newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura scandal spotlights need for reform -- panel.
newsitem.headline: Nomura scandal spotlights need for reform -- panel.

text.p: A scandal at Japan's Nomura Securities has had a silver lining for a panel working on reforms of the industry, by highlighting the need for change, a key member of the advisory body said on Friday.

"The scandal has given Japanese society and the securities industry itself the impression that reform of the securities industry is needed," said Shoichi Royama, a key member of the Securities and Exchange Council.
The council is an advisory panel to the finance minister and has been working on deregulation measures and other reforms of the securities industry.

Royama, also a professor at Osaka University, told reporters that the impact of the scandal at the nation's top brokerage was a "plus" in terms of the panel's debate. But he said he missed former Nomura vice president Atsushi Saito who resigned from the panel due to the scandal.
"We would like to establish a market in Japan which is sound, even if there are some troublesome brokers," he said.

Earlier on Friday the advisory panel released interim proposals for reforms in the securities business as part of the "Big Bang" drive for liberalised markets by 2001. It is scheduled to finalise its proposals next month.
In its report, the panel emphasised the need for a bigger team of securities regulators to monitor the industry and called for tougher penalties for illegal stock deals.
It also said Japan should move swiftly to liberalise commissions on stock transactions and should carry out the deregulation well before 2001.

But it added that initially, from April 1998, the liberalisation should only cover stock transactions above a certain threshold to smooth the transition to a deregulated market. It proposed a cut-off point below 100 million yen.
Royama also said that the question of securities houses setting up holding companies would be vigorously discussed in order to reach a final proposal in June.
